comments.author: BinaryIgor
comments.text: Related or not, sometimes I wonder whether we will ever come up with programming languages that both operate on a higher lever of abstraction that we currently have and are more productive in use. Java, Python, JavaScript and alikes are quite old; each level of abstraction give you a stronger lever but at the cost of losing more granular control; maybe the ones we currently have operate on the optimum abstraction level?

comments.author: andrewrogers
comments.text:
I think the fundamental issue is the retaining granular control requires the internals of abstractions to be highly complex in order to preserve the combinatorial complexity granular control implies. You can't hide the intrinsic complexity, only move it around. And the user still must have some understanding of what the abstraction invocation maps to.

One could argue that systems languages with strong metaprogramming features already provide this capability. In practice, very few developers have the metaprogramming skills required to build sufficiently powerful abstractions. I suspect this gap is more innate than we tend to acknowledge.

comments.author: Loup-Vaillant
comments.text:
In practice, very few developers have the metaprogramming skills required to build sufficiently powerful abstractions. I suspect this gap is more innate than we tend to acknowledge.


Hard to know until our education is actually up to snuff. Few of us come out of college with an understanding of how to actually decompose a program. Heck, most programmers these days are barely aware of the basic performance characteristics of our computers, or how much to expect of them.

At that scale, that’s not a cognitive disability, that’s an education, or perhaps curiosity, issue. Only once that’s out of the way, only once we actually teach the metaprogramming skills you speak of, will we know if the gap is that large. At least, among programmers who finished their degree.

comments.author: andrewrogers
comments.text:
Education and curiosity would certainly help, no disagreement on that point. I think this falls into a narrow case where it would help less than we would hope.

Even if we take education as a given, this particular aspect of development seems to run into the same "cognitive limits of systems thinking" that we run into in some physical engineering fields. There is a level of intrinsic complexity beyond which human brains stop reasoning well no matter how motivated. That threshold varies substantially across individuals but even rare outliers hit that wall sooner rather than later.

This is something AI might actually be able to help us with. They are less constrained by biological and evolutionary limits.

comments.author: dzwdz
comments.text:
I'll try to clarify myself, then. I was alluding to two separate things in my comment:


There's a vast chasm between what's legal and what's ethical. There are many reasons why I might want things I deem "bad" to regardless be legal: I might not think that the law can properly codify the nuances of when that thing is good, and when it's bad. I might not think it would be possible to enforce said law fairly. I might just prefer to trust people to do what they think is right, rather than using the state to threaten them with violence.


I believe that's been a pretty common idea in anti-copyright circles. The author of Unlicense wrote about it, for instance.


Realizations of ideas are distinct from ideas themselves. If someone discovers a good algorithm for something, you should be able to reimplement it freely. That's different from just taking their code and using it directly - there's a lot of work involved in actually implementing an idea, as we programmers are well aware of. (I'm not saying that should be illegal either - as mentioned, I would prefer to just trust people to not rip each other off, rather than try to enforce arbitrary restrictions on them.)


On another note, let's consider software patents. I don't think fair enforcement of patent law is possible. Two people can independently stumble upon the same idea; it makes no sense for the first of of them to "own" it exclusively. Thus, I'm opposed to software patents, or the "ownership" of ideas. Despite that, if your software heavily relies on the ideas of someone else, crediting them is still the right thing to do.
